title: Why we’re investing in Tomo
gist: Collab Fund announces an investment in Tomo, a consumer AI 'wellbeing' company that acts as a unified AI layer holding context across a user's finances, fitness, sleep, and stress. The thesis: durable consumer AI advantage comes from emotional trust and habit, and Tomo's 'forgiveness'/adaptive-interface design plus early traction (10,000+ paying subscribers in 3.5 months by word of mouth while in stealth) position it to define the category.

insights.claim: Even widely-used AI tools are 'one model release away from obsolescence,' so the durable advantage in consumer AI comes from products people emotionally trust, build habits around, and fold into their identities rather than from raw model capability.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: Frames the durable moat in consumer AI as trust/habit/identity rather than model performance — a lens for judging which AI-app startups can defend value as underlying models commoditize.
insights.quote: Even the beloved AI tools we already rely on are only one model release away from obsolescence.
insights.locator: Who will build the first era-defining

insights.claim: Generational consumer AI companies will be the ones people trust with their lives in full — not just their work — meaning the wellbeing/personal domain, not productivity, is where category-defining consumer AI will emerge.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: Signals where this VC expects the biggest consumer AI outcomes — personal/wellbeing over productivity — a directional bet for allocators screening the space.
insights.quote: Generational consumer AI companies will be the ones people trust with their lives — in all their fullness and chaos — not just their work.

insights.claim: Tomo positions as a unified AI layer holding context across a user's interconnected finances, fitness, sleep, and stress — contrasting with habit trackers, calorie counters, and budgeting apps that manage life in isolation and reward unbroken streaks.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: Defines Tomo's wedge against incumbent single-purpose self-tracking apps; the 'unified context layer' is the differentiator to validate versus fragmented competitors.
insights.quote: As a unified AI layer holding context across all of it, Tomo intervenes at the right moment to change behaviors and outcomes.
insights.locator: Habit trackers, calorie counters, and budgeting apps

insights.claim: 'Forgiveness' — allowing imperfect behavior to still count as a win (e.g. 'fries with dinner but no dessert counts as a win') — is framed as the retention mechanic the self-improvement app category has been missing.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: A non-obvious retention thesis: streak-based apps punish lapses and lose users; grace/forgiveness as a design mechanic is the claimed unlock for engagement in consumer wellbeing apps.
insights.quote: Forgiveness is the retention mechanic the category has been missing.
insights.locator: That context also allows for grace

insights.claim: Tomo ships adaptive interfaces that intuit and evolve with a user's changing needs — e.g. a race-training runner gets a training tracker; someone who can't get out of bed gets a game that unlocks only during their morning routine — deepening personalization and loyalty over time.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: The adaptive/personalized-interface approach is the mechanism claimed to compound loyalty; a differentiator to test against static single-feature apps.
insights.quote: Tomo delivers on a far-off promise of AI today by shipping adaptive interfaces that intuit user’s needs
insights.locator: Tomo delivers on a far-off promise

insights.claim: Tomo reached 10,000+ paying subscribers in three and a half months, entirely by word of mouth, while still in stealth.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: Paid-subscriber traction with zero paid marketing while in stealth is a strong product-market-fit signal — the core quantitative underwriting for the investment.
insights.quote: 10,000+ paying subscribers in three and a half months, entirely by word of mouth, while still in stealth.

insights.claim: Tomo users text the product 20 of every 30 days, engagement the firm says rivals the stickiest consumer apps.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: High daily-usage frequency (roughly two of every three days) supports the habit/retention thesis and is a key engagement benchmark for the investment case.
insights.quote: Users text Tomo 20 of every 30 days, engagement that rivals the stickiest consumer apps.
insights.locator: Users text Tomo 20 of every 30 days

insights.claim: Tomo's founders, Justin and Raymond, are described as intensely product-obsessed — dissecting divergent use cases through hours of user interviews and observation and inserting their own taste when needed.
insights.speaker: Craig Shapiro and Hamza Choudery
insights.so_what: Founder quality and product taste are named as a core part of the underwriting; relevant to assessing execution risk in a category-defining bet.
insights.quote: Justin and Raymond are as product-obsessed as founders get, dissecting divergent use cases through hours of interviews and observation
insights.locator: Justin and Raymond are as product-obsessed
